headline: The week the ten-year touched 5.365% and returned
standfirst: Weekend edition. The week in rates was a round trip: the ten-year touched 5.349% on Monday and 5.365% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002, then closed Thursday at 5.22% against 5.24% a week earlier, and the two-year at 4.75% against 4.78%. Each of the week's three auctions cleared at the highest yield in years, 4.932% for the three-year, 5.300% for the ten-year and 5.618% for the thirty-year, and each drew enough demand to pull yields back; the minutes said most Fed officials see another hike as likely appropriate by year-end, and futures price October as a hold at about 80% and December as a hike at about 70%. The S&P 500 gained 0.55% on the week and the Nasdaq Composite was flat, with records on Tuesday, while the Russell 2000 lost 1.37%; on Thursday the Nasdaq fell 1.25%, its biggest fall since mid-August, after a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualised revenue is about $20 billion below what investors were told. Brent rose about 4% on Thursday and fell 1.4% this morning after the president said the US will not strike Iran before the 3 November midterms. Korea's Kospi lost 5.4% on the week and is shut today with Taiwan. Ahead: Michigan sentiment today, the banks on Tuesday, CPI on Wednesday and the Fed on 28 October.

bullets.title: Rates: the ten-year touched 5.365% and ended 2bp lower than it began, through three auctions
bullets.text: The two-year closed Thursday at 4.75%, the ten-year at 5.22% and the thirty-year at 5.60%, against 4.78%, 5.24% and 5.61% a week earlier. The ten-year touched 5.349% on Monday after the ISM services prices-paid reading of 74.0 and 5.365% on Wednesday, and the thirty-year about 5.73%. The $58 billion three-year went at 4.932% on Tuesday, the highest since 2006, with a bid-to-cover of 2.62 and indirect bidders below average; the $39 billion ten-year at 5.300% on Wednesday, the highest since 2000, with 2.77 and indirect bidders taking about 80%; and the $22 billion thirty-year at 5.618% on Thursday, with 2.54 against a recent average near 2.4. Thursday's rally was led by the long end, with the 20-year-plus Treasury fund up 0.94% on the day and still down 4.72% over a month. The minutes of the September meeting showed all 19 participants backed the hike and most see another as likely appropriate by year-end; Waller said more hikes are needed but need not come immediately, and Jefferson has said more time may be needed. The Treasury market is shut on Monday for Columbus Day; CPI is on Wednesday.

bullets.title: Equities: records on Tuesday, a Nasdaq fall of 1.25% on Thursday, and a week that ended flat
bullets.text: The S&P 500 gained 0.55% on the week to 7,765.36, the Nasdaq Composite was flat at 27,193.34, the Dow gained 0.11% to 51,231.64 and the Russell 2000 lost 1.37%; the Nasdaq closed at records on Monday and Tuesday and the S&P 500 on Tuesday. On Thursday the Nasdaq lost 1.25%, its biggest fall since mid-August, after the Financial Times reported that OpenAI's annualised revenue was approaching $50 billion at the end of September against $70 billion reported by investors; Oracle fell about 5.5%, Nvidia 2.9% and AMD 3.9%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor index about 3.8% in the afternoon. The damage was narrow: more than two-thirds of S&P 500 members rose, energy gained 2.97% and consumer staples 2.11%, and technology fell 1.79%. Over the week energy gained 3.85%, staples 3.59% and utilities 3.11%, while technology lost 1.02% and industrials 0.91%. The third-quarter earnings season starts today with Delta, and JPMorgan, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report on Tuesday; consensus has S&P 500 earnings up about 29.5% on the year, according to FactSet via AJ Bell.

bullets.title: Oil and Iran: Brent rose 4% on Thursday, then fell after a pledge of no strikes before the midterms
bullets.text: December Brent is $102.83, down 1.39% this morning and up 0.57% on the week, and WTI $90.29, down 1.31% and 0.90% lower on the week. Brent settled near $104.3 on Thursday, up about 4%, after reports that the Pentagon had prepared plans for three days of strikes on Iranian targets, nine tanker attacks near Hormuz in a week, and a hurricane that led Gulf of Mexico producers to shut in about 1.3 million barrels a day, according to FXStreet. It fell this morning after the president said the US would not attack Iran before the 3 November midterm elections and that talks were productive, while keeping the naval blockade of Iranian ports; Vice President Vance said Iran must cut its enrichment capacity, and Iran's atomic energy chief rejected giving it up. Heating oil is up 7.00% on the week. The Brent 1M column still straddles the 30 September roll to December.

bullets.title: Europe, Asia and the dollar: France and Korea led the declines, and the dollar heads for a fourth weekly gain
bullets.text: The Stoxx 600 closed Thursday at 625.51, down 0.93% on the week, the DAX 1.7% lower, the CAC 40 2.1% and Italy's FTSE MIB 2.4%. French ten-year yields touched 4.92% in the week; euro-area finance ministers and the ECB told France to pass a 2027 budget, and Bloomberg reported that Lagarde told ministers the ECB can counter disorderly moves if certain criteria are met. The euro is $1.12, up 0.64% on the week after a 16-month low near $1.116 on Monday, and the dollar is on course for a fourth straight weekly gain, according to Investing.com. The Kospi lost 5.39% on the week, with Samsung Electronics guiding to a record third-quarter profit but foreign investors selling, and is shut today with Taiwan; the Nikkei is down 0.24% this morning, Hong Kong up 1.09% and Shanghai down 1.21% on reopening. India's central bank hiked to 5.5% on Wednesday; Brazil's Bovespa gained 7.34% on the week.

bullets.title: Gold, crypto and what is on today: gold at a weekly high, Bitcoin down 4.7% on the week, Michigan at 10:00 ET
bullets.text: Gold is $4,222.80, up 1.58% this morning and 1.45% on the week, after touching a two-month low near $4,066 on Wednesday; silver is up 2.32% and platinum 2.45%. Bitcoin is $82,437, up 0.91% this morning and down 4.71% on the week, Ether down 8.54% and Solana 9.06%. Today brings Canada's unemployment rate at 08:30 ET, seen 6.5% after 6.4%, and the preliminary Michigan sentiment survey at 10:00 ET, seen 47.6 after 48.1, with September's one-year inflation expectations at 4.6% and five-year at 3.4%; the New York Fed's survey this week showed one-year expectations at the highest in more than three years. Delta reports this morning, and Reuters lists ECB speakers Cipollone and Schnabel and Brazil's September inflation. Korea and Taiwan are shut.

calendar.note: Seen 6.5% after 6.4%. The Bank of Canada is at 2.25% and decides on 28 October with a policy report and press conference; oil pass-through argues for a hike and a rising jobless rate against.
Seen 47.6 after 48.1. One-year inflation expectations were 4.6% and five-year 3.4%, and the expectations line is the one the Fed will read. Delta reports this morning.

calendar.event: Columbus Day: US bond market closed; Hammack 12:50 ET
calendar.note: Equities trade; Treasuries and the banks do not. The IMF and World Bank meetings run in Washington through the week. The RBA's minutes follow at 20:30 ET.

calendar.event: JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citigroup report
calendar.note: JPMorgan at 08:30, Goldman at 09:30, Wells Fargo at 10:00 and Citigroup at 11:00 ET, the start of the banks. UBS expects JPMorgan, Goldman and Citigroup, among others, to miss estimates in a rising-yield environment. German final HICP is at 02:00 ET.
The first CPI after the September hike: August was 3.4% on the year with the monthly at +0.4%, and core +0.3% on the month. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report; the Beige Book is at 14:00 ET.

calendar.event: US retail sales, PPI, claims and the Philadelphia Fed
calendar.note: Retail sales rose 1.2% in August with the control group at +1.4%; core PPI was 4.6% on the year. Hammack speaks at 16:30 ET and Australia's jobs report is out overnight on Wednesday.

calendar.event: Empire State survey; industrial production 09:15 ET; Bailey speaks
calendar.note: The Bank of England's Bailey speaks at the IMF meetings (02:00 UTC, the evening before in New York). China's GDP, retail sales and industrial production follow on the 19th.

calendar.event: Fed decision; Bank of Canada 09:45 ET
calendar.note: The first Fed meeting since the September hike, with the press conference at 14:30 ET. The Bank of Canada decides at 09:45 ET with a policy report; Australia's CPI is out at 20:30 ET the evening before and the ECB decides on the 29th.

sessionNote: The weekend edition covers a week in which very little ended far from where it began: the ten-year, the two-year and the S&P 500 finished within a few basis points or half a percent of last Friday, yet each had a sharp move in between. The market's open questions are the ones the week did not settle: the minutes say most officials see another hike by year-end without a date, futures lean to a hold on 28 October and a hike in December, and CPI on Wednesday is the first hard data. Thursday's AI shock was narrow, but it came with the earnings season due to start today. The oil and Iran reports have swung twice this week, and the president's pledge applies only until 3 November. Korea and Taiwan reopen Monday; the US bond market is shut Monday for Columbus Day while equities trade.
watchOut: Reading a flat week as a calm one. The ten-year touched 5.365% and ended 2bp lower than it began, the Nasdaq made a record and its worst day since August within three sessions, and Brent has moved 4% in a day on headlines that reversed within a day; the closing numbers hide ranges that were wide. Second, the OpenAI report: it is a Financial Times report of documents shared with backers, not a company statement, and Thursday's move was concentrated in AI infrastructure names while two-thirds of the S&P 500 rose. Third, Monday: with the bond market shut, Treasury yields do not trade on the day, so the first cash read after the weekend is Tuesday, with the banks reporting. Fourth, the Brent 1M column still straddles the 30 September roll. Fifth, the pledge of no strikes on Iran before 3 November is a statement by one official, made the day after reports of strike planning. Size for CPI on Wednesday, not for the weekend.

archive.headline: Nasdaq record. Ten-year at a 24-year high.
archive.summary: Brazil's Ibovespa jumped 7.7% to a record after Flavio Bolsonaro led the presidential first round, the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 27,477.31 on Nvidia and the S&P 500 at 7,773.95. ISM services prices paid rose to 74.0, the highest since July 2022, and the ten-year touched 5.349%, its highest since 2002, before closing near 5.31%. Brent fell about 2% to $100.3 on a G7 stock release, and the euro touched a 17-month low near $1.116 on French and Spanish politics.

archive.headline: Payrolls 29,000. Yields rose anyway.
archive.summary: September payrolls rose 29,000 against about 90,000 expected with a net 60,000 downward revision, unemployment 4.2% and wages +0.1%; October's Fed hike went to about 22% priced and the Nasdaq touched a record, but the ten-year closed about 3bp higher after Logan said half a point more is needed. The G7 agreed a 100 million barrel stock release, euro-area inflation printed 3.8%, Tokyo core CPI 2.7% and the dollar index reached a 17-month high.

archive.headline: Payrolls 29,000. Yields rose anyway.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. October's Fed hike went from more than 70% priced on Monday to about 25% by Thursday on Williams, a 3.0% core PCE and Jefferson, while the long end set 2002 highs on a 2.2% GDP revision, a 58.8 Chicago PMI and ISM prices paid at 77.9; the ten-year touched 5.344% and closed 5.233%. Brent rose 4.4% on China's fuel-export halt and a third US carrier group, Nike cut its guidance, the euro hit a 16-month low on France's budget and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7%.
